Inversion In Circle And Isosceles 2

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Move three points on a line and watch the circle squeezed between two others.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes and press a Step button to uncover the proof.
Look for the math

The small orange circle is tucked between a big circle, a smaller circle and a slanted line. Move the three points and its centre always stays directly above B. Here is why, with no lengths to work out — the page calls this solution remarkable for having no calculations at all. (The program still computes where to draw the circle; the proof is the calculation-free part.) The live cut-the-knot page still carries the whole proof but has its Java applet tag commented out; a 2010 Wayback capture shows the working InversionInCircleAndIsosceles2 applet this port follows.

A rhombus and an incenter

The big circle has AC as its diameter and the smaller one has AB. The line through the middle of BC, straight up and down, cuts the big circle at E and F. That makes BECF a rhombus, and so BE = EC. Press Step 1: EB and FB meet the circle again at K and L, and the line FE cuts the angle at F in half. From that, EL = EC = EB, so B is the incenter of triangle CKL.

Where the orange circle sits

Step 2 draws the upright line through B. It cuts the big circle at M and N, so the circle centred at B through M meets the big circle at opposite ends of a diameter. Write t = AB/AC. The orange circle has radius AC · t(1−t)/(1+t) and its centre is AC · t/(1+t) · √(2(1−t)) above B. Those are the applet's own formulas; they make the circle touch the big circle, the smaller circle and the line BE. Its centre has exactly B's x-coordinate, so BQ is perpendicular to AC — the claim the page asks us to prove.

Inversion with a negative power

Now invert in a circle centred at B with negative power −BM² = −BA·BC (the inversion page calls this inversion with a negative power). The big circle comes back to itself, the line EBK comes back to itself, and A and C swap places. The circle with diameter AB goes to the upright line through C, which is an external angle bisector of triangle CKL.

Feuerbach finishes it

Steps 3 and 4 name the excenters I_k and I_l. The inverse of the orange circle is a circle touching I_kI_l, touching BE, and (by Feuerbach's theorem) touching the nine-point circle of triangle BI_kI_l — which is the big circle. So it is the excircle at B, centred on the external bisector of the angle at B. That bisector is upright, while BC lies along the baseline; hence BQQ' is perpendicular to AC.

The logic test checks all of these equalities for 300 configurations of A, B and C, and matches every constructed point against a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode: the largest error is below one millionth of a drawing unit. The sibling applet Tangent Circles and an Isosceles Triangle proves the same claim with ordinary positive-power inversion and a Pythagorean sum; this one uses negative power and Feuerbach, and has five Step screens rather than six.

Turn on the names, press Step 4, and drag B: watch Q and Q' slide along the same upright line while the big circle stays put. What happens as B approaches A?
